testCases.testName: Verify SCPC is fully enabled running Type Cover Disable

testScenarios.objective:
In TestingScript.xml, the Type Cover Disable test is described as:
“Verify the Type Cover is enabled. Then it disables the Type Cover and verifies it is disabled. Finally, it re-enables the Type Cover and verifies it is enabled.”
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
In TypeCoverDisable.ps1, the script first validates the DUT configuration, creates the required scheduled task if needed, and reboots to restore the default state if the SEMM setting is already disabled.
It checks whether the Type Cover is connected. If a Type Cover is found while the setting is enabled, it proceeds to disable the Type Cover setting through SEMM.
After the disable step, it verifies that the Type Cover is no longer present and records a result for “Verify the Type cover is present.”
It then reboots/enters UEFI, re-enables the Type Cover through SEMM, and verifies that the Type Cover is present again after re-enabling.
Separately, in SCPC.psm1, the SCPC security verification scans SCPC verifier logs associated with the Type Cover Disable test and records the overall SCPC security result.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass:
The Type Cover is initially detected when it should be enabled, disappears after the disable operation, and is detected again after re-enabling.
For the SCPC security objective, the matching SCPC verifier logs for the Type Cover Disable test do not contain “FAILED,” so the result is recorded as Pass.
Fail:
No Type Cover is found when it should be present, the Type Cover remains present after the disable operation, or the Type Cover does not reappear after re-enabling.
For the SCPC security objective, if any matching verifier log for the test contains “FAILED,” the result is recorded as Fail.

testCases.testName: Verify SCPC is fully enabled running Verify Enterprise Enrollment

testScenarios.objective:
In TestingScript.xml, the test description for Verify Enterprise Enrollment is:
“The script is verifying the items in the list: The Win32_SystemEnclosure matches the SMBIOSBIOSVersion, and the system is configured with UEFI. The Bios Serial and System Enclosure Serial number match, and a SecureBoot Test has been performed. The Bitlocker status is On with XtsAes128 and XtsAes256 encryption, and the KeyProtector is set to Tpm and RecoveryPassword. The system is fully encrypted with Bitlocker. DeviceGuard is enabled with CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus. Hyper V is both on and off, indicating a change in status. The operating system is a Windows Enterprise Edition. The TPM is present, ready, enabled, and owned. The system is commercial and enrolled in Fabrikam.”
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
In VerifyEnterpriseEnrollment.ps1, the script first ensures SCPC is in the default state before verification; if SCPC is OFF, it turns it ON and requires the verification script to be run again.
It collects and checks device configuration data from the system using WMI/CIM/PowerShell, including:
Computer model, OS build and edition, BIOS version, serial number consistency, Secure Boot state, BitLocker state and encryption method, BitLocker key protectors, encryption percentage, DeviceGuard status, Hyper-V status, Windows edition, TPM presence/readiness/enabled/owned state, device commercial status, and Fabrikam enrollment.
The script writes each check into the verification results log with Pass/Fail status.
Separately, the SCPCSecurity routine in SCPC.psm1 scans the SCPC verifier logs for the Verify Enterprise Enrollment test and records the overall SCPCSecurity result as Pass or Fail.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass if:
Win32_SystemEnclosure matches SMBIOSBIOSVersion.
BIOS serial and system enclosure serial numbers match.
Secure Boot is enabled.
BitLocker is On, uses a supported encryption method of XtsAes128 or XtsAes256, includes Tpm and RecoveryPassword protectors, and shows 100% encryption.
DeviceGuard/VBS and CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus are enabled where supported.
Hyper-V is enabled where supported.
Windows edition is Enterprise.
TPM is present, ready, enabled, and owned.
The device is commercial and enrolled in Fabrikam.
The SCPC verifier log for this test exists and does not contain FAILED.
Fail if:
Any of the required device checks above do not pass.
The matching SCPC verifier log contains FAILED.

testCases.testName: Verify SCPC is fully enabled running Wake On Lan

testScenarios.objective:
In TestingScript.xml, the Wake On Lan test is described as:
“Verify the Wake On Lan is enabled. Then it disables the Wake On Lan and verifies it is disabled. Finally, it re-enables the Wake On Lan and verifies it is enabled.”
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The script in WakeOnLan.ps1 first validates the DUT setup and creates the required scheduled task if needed.
If the SEMM state is already enabled, it disables the Wake On Lan setting and reboots so the DUT starts from the disabled state.
It then checks the state after the first disable step and records whether the Wake On Lan SEMM setting is disabled.
It re-enables the Wake On Lan setting through SEMM, reboots, and checks whether the setting is enabled.
It then disables the setting again, reboots, and performs a final validation that the setting is disabled again.
Separately, the SCPC security verification routine in SCPC.psm1 checks the matching SCPC verifier logs and records a Pass/Fail result for the overall SCPCSecurity objective.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass if:
After the first disable step, the Wake On Lan SEMM setting is observed as Disabled.
After the re-enable step, the Wake On Lan SEMM setting is observed as Enabled.
After the final disable step, the Wake On Lan SEMM setting is again observed as Disabled.
For the SCPCSecurity objective, the matching verifier log for this test exists and does not contain “FAILED.”
Fail if:
The setting is still Enabled when it should be Disabled, or still Disabled when it should be Enabled.
Any of the validation checks above do not match the expected state.
For the SCPCSecurity objective, the matching verifier log contains “FAILED.”

testCases.testName: Verify SCPC is fully enabled running Wifi

testScenarios.objective:
In TestingScript.xml, the Wi‑Fi test is described as:
“Verify Wifi is enabled. Then it disables Wifi and verifies it is disabled. Finally, it re-enables the Wifi and verifies it is enabled.”
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The script in Wifi.ps1 first ensures the DUT is configured correctly and sets the Wi‑Fi setting to the default state if needed.
It then attempts to disable Wi‑Fi through SEMM, reboots, and checks that the Wi‑Fi adapter is no longer present/active during the disabled state.
It re-enables Wi‑Fi through SEMM, reboots again, and checks that the Wi‑Fi adapter is present/active after re-enabling.
The script records results for:
Stage 1: Wi‑Fi is present before disabling.
Stage 2: Wi‑Fi is not present after disabling.
Stage 3: Wi‑Fi is present again after re-enabling.
Separately, the SCPC security verification logic in SCPC.psm1 checks the matching SCPC verifier logs for the Wi‑Fi test and records the overall SCPCSecurity result as Pass or Fail.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass if:
The Wi‑Fi adapter is detected as present before the disable step.
After the disable step, the Wi‑Fi adapter is not present/available, confirming it was disabled.
After the re-enable step, the Wi‑Fi adapter is present again, confirming it was re-enabled.
For the SCPCSecurity objective, the matching verifier log for this test exists and does not contain “FAILED.”
Fail if:
The Wi‑Fi adapter is not present when it should be present before the disable step.
The Wi‑Fi adapter is still present after the disable step when it should have been disabled.
The Wi‑Fi adapter is not present again after the re-enable step when it should be enabled.
For the SCPCSecurity objective, the matching verifier log contains “FAILED.”

testCases.testName: Verify SCPC is fully enabled running Wifi BT

testScenarios.objective:
In TestingScript.xml, the test description is:
“Verify Wifi and BT are enabled. Then it disables the Wifi and BT and verifies they are disabled. Finally, it re-enables the Wifi and BT and verifies they are enabled.”
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
In WifiBt.ps1, the script first validates that the DUT is configured correctly and creates the needed scheduled task.
If the SEMM state is already disabled, it re-enables the Wi‑Fi/BT setting to restore the default state and reboots the device.
In the first execution stage, it checks whether Wi‑Fi hardware is present, disables the Wi‑Fi/BT setting through SEMM, reboots, and records whether the initial presence check passed.
In the second stage, it re-checks the post-disable state after reboot:
it verifies that Bluetooth is not present, and
it verifies that Wi‑Fi is not present.
In the third stage, it re-enables the Wi‑Fi/BT setting, reboots again, and verifies:
Bluetooth is present again, and
Wi‑Fi is present again.
Separately, the SCPC security verification routine in SCPC.psm1 scans the matching SCPC verifier logs for the Wifi BT test and records the overall SCPCSecurity result as Pass or Fail.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass if:
Wi‑Fi is detected as present before the disable step.
After the disable step, Bluetooth is no longer present and Wi‑Fi is no longer present.
After the re-enable step, Bluetooth is present again and Wi‑Fi is present again.
For the SCPCSecurity objective, the matching verifier log for this test exists and does not contain “FAILED”.

Wi‑Fi is not present when it should be present before the disable step.
Bluetooth or Wi‑Fi is still present after the disable step when it should have been disabled.
Bluetooth or Wi‑Fi is not present again after the re-enable step when it should be enabled.
For the SCPCSecurity objective, the matching verifier log contains “FAILED”.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SDCard

testScenarios.objective:
Based on the local source under the EnterpriseEnrollment folder, this objective is a post-test validation check for the SDcard test. Its purpose is to confirm that running the SDcard SEMM enable/disable flow does not leave any additional devices or drivers in a bad state after the test completes.
The check is implemented in TestFunctionality.psm1 and is applied around the SDcard workflow in SDCard.ps1.
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Start the SDcard test and verify that the SDcard is present at stage 0; if it is missing, the test is treated as failed at the initial setup stage.
If the SDcard is present, schedule the required task and, if needed, reboot to set the SDcard reader to the default state.
In the next stage, disable the SDcard through the SEMM package, write the stage status, and reboot.
In the follow-up stage, verify that the SDcard is no longer present; if it is still present, record a failure for the “Verify SDCard is not present” condition.
Re-enable the SDcard and reboot again, then verify that the SDcard is present again; if it is not present, record a failure for the “Verify SDCard is present” condition.
After the SDcard test reaches a stage beyond the initial setup, the shared verification logic checks whether any new devices/drivers entered a bad state compared with what was already present at the start of the test.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass:
No additional devices or drivers are found in a bad state after the SDcard test beyond those already present at the start of the test.
If a device error is known and explicitly marked as an ignored known bug, it does not cause a failure.
Fail:
Any additional device or driver is found in a bad state after the SDcard test and is not part of the known ignore list.
When this happens, the framework logs a failure for the objective “No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SDCard” and records the affected device names and statuses in the test log.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SDCardTest

testScenarios.objective: I did not find a literal objective named “No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SDCardTest” in the local EnterpriseEnrollment source. The corresponding SDcard validation is implemented as a generic post-test check in TestFunctionality.psm1 and is applied during the SDcard test flow in SDCard.ps1. Its purpose is to ensure that the SDcard enable/disable sequence does not leave any additional devices or drivers in a bad state.
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At stage 0, verify that the SDcard is detected; if it is not present, mark the setup as failed and stop the flow.
If the SDcard is present, create the required scheduled task and reboot if needed to restore the SDcard reader to its default state before continuing.
In stage 1, disable the SDcard through the SEMM package, update the test stage tracker, and reboot.
In stage 2, verify that the SDcard is no longer present; if it is still present, record a failure for the “Verify SDCard is not present” check, then re-enable the SDcard and reboot.
In stage 3, verify that the SDcard is present again; if it is not, record a failure for the “Verify SDCard is present” check.
After the test has progressed beyond the initial setup, the shared framework logic compares the device/driver state after the SDcard flow against the state captured at the start of the test and records the objective result.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass:
No additional devices or drivers are found in a bad state after the SDcard test beyond those already present at the start of the test.
If the condition is caused by a known device-driver bug that the local ignore logic recognizes, it does not count as a failure.
Fail:
Any additional device or driver is found in a bad state after the SDcard test and is not covered by the known-bug ignore list.
When that happens, the framework logs a failure for the objective and records the affected device names and statuses in the test log.

testCases.testName: No new drivers not OK at start of: SDCard

testScenarios.objective:
This objective is a shared pre/post-device-state check for the SDcard test. In the local EnterpriseEnrollment source, it is implemented in GeneralFunctions.psm1 and is invoked from the common test framework path used by the SDcard test flow in SDCard.ps1.
The check records whether the SDcard test introduced any new device drivers whose status was not “OK” at the start of the test. Its purpose is to ensure the SDcard SEMM enable/disable flow did not create additional driver-state problems.
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At the start of the test, capture the baseline device-driver state from the system by gathering all PnP entities whose status is not “OK” and whose config manager error code is greater than 0.
Compare that initial list with the set of drivers already known to be not OK from prior runs by reading the stored “DriversNotOK” environment variable.
Filter out any drivers that were already present in that baseline list, leaving only newly discovered drivers that are not OK.
If new not-OK drivers are found, log them and write a result for the objective; otherwise, log a passing result for the objective.
This check runs as part of the test framework setup/validation flow before the SDcard-specific stages continue.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass:
No new drivers appear in a not-OK state during the SDcard test beyond those already present in the baseline list from the start of the test.
If the test is the EnterpriseEnrollment root test, the framework uses a special case behavior that treats the baseline as “all drivers OK at start of” and does not flag the initial baseline list as a failure.
Fail:
One or more new drivers appear with status not “OK” and a positive config manager error code during the SDcard test, and they were not already present in the baseline list.
When this occurs, the framework writes a failure result named “No new drivers not OK at start of: <TestName>” and logs the affected driver names, status, and device ID details.

testCases.testName: No new drivers not OK at start of: SDCardTest

testScenarios.objective:
This objective is implemented as a shared helper check in the local EnterpriseEnrollment source, not as a separate SDcard-only script. The logic comes from GeneralFunctions.psm1 and is invoked during the common test initialization path used by the SDcard flow in SDCard.ps1.
Its purpose is to detect whether the SDcard test causes any new device drivers to appear in a not-OK state compared with the baseline state captured at the start of the test.
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At the beginning of the test run, the framework gathers the current device-driver list from the system and selects those with a status other than “OK” and a config manager error code greater than 0.
It compares those found drivers against the baseline list already stored in the user environment variable “DriversNotOK” from prior execution state.
Drivers that were already present in that baseline are ignored; only newly discovered not-OK drivers remain for evaluation.
If any new not-OK drivers are found, the framework logs them with their caption, status, and device ID and writes an objective result for the test name.
If no such new drivers are found, the framework logs a passing result for the objective.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass:
No new drivers appear in a not-OK state during the SDcard test beyond what was already present in the baseline set captured at the start.
The objective passes if the device-driver state remains unchanged relative to that initial baseline.
Fail:
One or more new drivers appear with a status other than “OK” and a positive config manager error code that were not already in the baseline list.
When that happens, the framework writes a failure result named “No new drivers not OK at start of: <TestName>” and logs the affected driver details.

testCases.testName: Confirm change in brightness

testScenarios.objective: Confirm change in brightness
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Connect the device to AC power before starting the test.
Install the Surface Brightness Control application and verify that the brightness-control service is present and running.
Verify the relevant registry/settings values for the service, including:
service enabled,
brightness adjustment on AC power behavior,
default low brightness value,
default high brightness value,
inactivity timeout,
telemetry setting.
Let the system wait for the screen to dim under the default configuration and observe whether the brightness changes.
Disconnect power and observe whether the screen dims on battery power.
Reconnect AC power and observe whether the screen brightens.
Re-enable the AC-power brightness adjustment setting, reboot, and verify that dimming occurs within the expected time.
Uninstall the brightness-control application and confirm that the service is no longer running.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass:
The brightness-control service is installed and running.
The registry/settings match the expected values for default brightness behavior and timeout.
The screen does not dim under default AC-power settings.
The screen dims on battery power.
The screen brightens when AC power is attached.
After enabling AC-power brightness adjustment, the screen dims within the expected time window.
After uninstall, the brightness-control service is no longer running.
Fail:
The service is missing or not running.
The registry/settings do not match the expected brightness-control values.
The screen does not dim or brighten when expected.
The screen remains at the wrong brightness level under the tested power state.
The service still remains running after uninstall.

testCases.testName: Connect a Type-C device and confirm it was found?

testScenarios.objective: Connect a Type-C device and confirm it was found?
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Confirm the device under test is configured for the USB-C test and that the supported USB-C SEMM IDs are enabled.
Remove all USB-C devices from the system and let the device list settle.
Connect a USB 3.0 device to the enabled USB-C port and observe whether it enumerates on the system.
Disconnect the USB 3.0 device, then connect a USB 2.0 device to the same USB-C port and observe whether it enumerates.
Remove all attached devices and connect a USB 4.0 dock/device to verify whether it is detected and whether it charges the DUT and/or works as a monitor/audio endpoint where applicable.
Record the result based on whether the device count increases or the expected USB-C behavior is observed.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass:
The connected USB 3.0 or USB 2.0 device appears on the system, and the USB device count increases compared with the empty-port baseline.
For a USB 4.0 dock/device, the test is marked pass when the device is detected and charging/monitor/audio behavior works as expected where supported.
Fail:
The connected device does not enumerate on the system, which causes the script to record the corresponding result as “Fail”.
The script logs failure conditions such as “USB 3.0 device connected to enabled USB-C port did not enumerate” or “No devices were added on USBC port.”

testCases.testName: SCPC: Stage 2 Verify USB, Ethernet and Audio are disabled:

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: Stage 2 Verify USB, Ethernet and Audio are disabled:
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Configure the Semm Dock to disable USB, Ethernet, and Audio ports for all users (both authorized and unauthorized users)
Wait for the Dock to reset and complete configuration (15 seconds)
Verify the status of three components through WMI queries:
USB Hub status
Audio Codec status
Ethernet Controller status
If any ports are still enabled, prompt the user to detach and reattach the dock for a second authorization attempt
Recheck the port status after dock reattachment

testCases.testName: SCPC: Stage 3 Verify Authorization. USB, Ethernet and Audio are enabled:

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: Stage 3 Verify Authorization. USB, Ethernet and Audio are enabled:
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Configure the Semm Dock to enable USB, Ethernet, and Audio ports only for Authorized Users (disable for unauthorized users)
Apply the provisioning configuration with:
Authorized User Audio: Enabled
Authorized User USB: Enabled
Authorized User Ethernet: Enabled
Unauthorized User Audio: Disabled
Unauthorized User USB: Disabled
Unauthorized User Ethernet: Disabled
Wait for the Dock to reset and complete configuration (15 seconds)
Verify the status of three components through WMI queries:
USB Hub status
Audio Codec status
Ethernet Controller status
Count the total number of enabled ports
If the count is not 3, prompt the user to detach and reattach the dock for a second authorization attempt
Recheck the port status after dock reattachment

testCases.testName: SCPC: Stage 4 Attached dock back to original DUT

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: Stage 4 Attached dock back to original DUT
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Step 1: Disconnect the dock from the original device and attach it to a second Surface device
Step 2: On the second device, open the Surface App
Step 3: On the second device, navigate to Dock → Port Status and wait 10 seconds for port status to refresh
Step 4: Verify on the second device if USB is available for charging only (for unauthorized user)
Step 5: Verify on the second device if Ethernet is unavailable (for unauthorized user)
Step 6: Verify on the second device if Audio is unavailable (for unauthorized user)
Step 7: Attach the dock back to the original test device
Wait for the dock to reset and be detected (15 seconds)
Verify the status of the three components (USB Hub, Audio Codec, Ethernet Controller) on the original device through WMI queries
Count the total number of enabled ports
If the count is not 3, prompt the user to detach and reattach the dock for a second verification attempt
Recheck the port status after dock reattachment

testCases.testName: SCPC: Stage 5 Verify USB, Ethernet and Audio are enabled:

testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Read the current dock provisioning status.
Log that the test is verifying USB, Ethernet, and Audio are enabled.
Count how many of the three ports are currently enabled.
If the count is not 3, attempt recovery:
If only Ethernet is disabled, prompt for a dock power reset and reconnect.
Reconfigure the dock with all USB, Ethernet, and Audio permissions enabled for authorized and unauthorized users.
Wait for the dock to reset.
Re-check the port status.
If the ports are enabled after the recovery step, mark the test as passed and continue.
If the ports are still not enabled, log a failure and stop the test flow.

testCases.testName: Stage 1 Verify USB, Ethernet and Audio are enabled:

Read the current dock provisioning status.
Log that the test is verifying USB, Ethernet, and Audio are enabled.
Count the current enabled state of the three components:
USB Hub
Audio Codec
Ethernet Controller
If all three are not enabled, attempt remediation:
If only Ethernet is disabled, prompt for a dock power-cycle reset because the script identifies this as a known issue.
Reconfigure the dock with USB, Ethernet, and Audio enabled for both authorized and unauthorized users.
Wait for the dock to reset.
Re-check the enabled state of the three components.
If the ports are still not enabled after the remediation attempt, log a failure and stop the test flow.
If all three ports are enabled, mark the stage as passed and advance to the next stage.

testCases.testName: LSV protection working

testScenarios.objective: LSV protection working
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Send a SEMM package that sets a target setting (example: setting ID 603 / Wake on Power) and log the current LSV; reboot the system.
After reboot, attempt to install a SEMM package using an older LSV timestamp (one year old) via Send-SemmPackage with -LSVOverRide set to the older DateTime; reboot again.
Retrieve the latest LSV state via UEFI_LSV_Change and check whether the LSV value changed as a result of the old package attempt.
Optionally run Write-Log and other diagnostic messages to record package/status values; the script also prints permission/package status from $testDataObject.UEFI.
The script advances test stages, reboots between stages, and performs final cleanup after verification.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SemmLsv

testScenarios.objective: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SemmLsv
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Run during test startup/boot path inside Get-TestStarted for the current test (SemmLsv).
Read the initial list of drivers-not-OK saved at test start from the environment variable DriversNotOK.
Enumerate current drivers with errors using Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" -and $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }.
Compute the difference: filter out drivers that were already not-OK at test start to produce additionalDevicesInBadState.
Call IsKnownDeviceDriverBug to exclude any expected/ignored driver failures for this test.
If any unexpected additional bad drivers remain, log each device (name and status) and mark the objective result; otherwise mark it passed.

After test actions, call NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState to:
Enumerate current drivers with Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" -and $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }.
Filter out drivers present in the baseline DriversNotOK list to produce additionalDevicesInBadState.
Pass the findings through IsKnownDeviceDriverBug to ignore expected/known driver issues for this test.
The calling script (SemmLsv.ps1) logs any unexpected drivers and records the result.

testCases.testName: SCPC: LSV protection working

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: LSV protection working
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Send a SEMM package to update a setting (e.g., setting ID 603) and reboot to apply it.
After reboot, try to install a SEMM package using an older LSV timestamp (one year old) via Send-SemmPackage -LSVOverRide <oldDate> and reboot.
Retrieve the LSV change state via UEFI_LSV_Change (the script stores the result in $LSV_State).
Based on $LSV_State, determine whether the LSV changed after the old-package attempt.
Record the result to the test results log and reboot/cleanup as the script directs.

Subtract the baseline list to get additionalDevicesInBadState.

testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: No unexpected new drivers are found in a non-OK state after the test (i.e., NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState returns true or any findings are classified as known/ignored bugs). The test result is written as a Pass.
Fail: One or more unexpected new drivers are found in a non-OK state (i.e., NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState returns false and they are not exempted by IsKnownDeviceDriverBug). The script logs details and writes a Fail.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SMT

testScenarios.objective: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SMT
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
When SMT.ps1 begins, it calls Get-TestStarted and establishes the current test stage.
On the initial stage (TestStage 0), shared logic calls Set_DriversNotOK_EnvironmentVariable -TestName $testName.
That function enumerates Win32_PNPEntity devices with Status -ne "OK" and ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0.
It saves the names of those baseline non-OK drivers into the DriversNotOK environment variable.
On later test execution after the initial stage, shared logic calls NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState.
NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState re-enumerates current non-OK drivers and excludes those present in the baseline list.
If any remaining new bad-state drivers are found, it checks IsKnownDeviceDriverBug to ignore expected known issues.
The framework then writes the result as No additional devices ended up in bad state in: SMT.

It re-enumerates current non-OK drivers and excludes any names already recorded in the baseline.

The result is written as No additional devices ended up in bad state in: $TestName.

testCases.testName: SCPC: The SMT test

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: The SMT test
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Start the SMT test and obtain $testDataObject and $TestStage via Get-TestStarted.
Stage 0:
If SMT is already disabled, re-enable it and reboot to set the device to default state.
Advance to Stage 1 and reboot.
Stage 1:
Start AutoKVM UEFI capture if available.
Record the current number of processors.
Disable SMT using Send-SemmPackage -SettingState $false.
Advance to Stage 2 and reboot.
Stage 2:
If automated, verify AutoKVM expected output False for Enable SMT.
Count processors again and compare to the pre-disable value.
If the count is lower, write Verify SMT is not present as Pass; otherwise write it as Fail.
Re-enable SMT with Send-SemmPackage -SettingState $true.
Advance to Stage 3 and reboot.
Stage 3:
If automated, verify AutoKVM expected output True for Enable SMT.
Count processors after re-enabling SMT.
Compare the processor count to the count recorded before disabling.
If the count matches, write Verify SMT is present as Pass; otherwise write it as Fail.
Clean up and end the test.

testCases.testName: SCPC: Verify SMT is not present

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: Verify SMT is not present
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At Stage 2, the script checks whether AutoKVM is active by testing for the AutoKVMLog.
If automated, it calls Get-AutoKVMPassFail -TestName "Enable SMT" -TestResultsFileName $testDataObject.TestResultsLogName -DesiredOutput "False".
It reads the current processor count from env:NUMBER_OF_PROCESSORS.
It reads the saved processor count from before disabling SMT using Read-TestStatus($ProcessorLog).
It compares the current processor count to the pre-disable count.
If the current count is lower, it writes Verify SMT is not present as Pass in SMTResults.log.
If the current count is not lower, it writes Verify SMT is not present as Fail in SMTResults.log.
It then re-enables SMT with Send-SemmPackage -SettingState $true and advances to Stage 3.

testCases.testName: Confirm the install button is disabled?

testScenarios.objective: This test validates that the Surface Brightness Control application installs correctly and operates with the expected default behavior. It confirms the service is running, the registry configuration is correct, and the screen responds properly to AC power and battery power conditions. It is a functional validation of the Surface Dimmer app rather than a UI button-state check.
testScenarios.detailedSteps: Ensure the device is connected to AC power before starting the test. Install the Surface Brightness Control MSI package from the test resource path. Wait for the service to start. Confirm the Surface Brightness service is running. Check the required registry values for service enablement and default brightness settings. Validate the default behavior when connected to AC power: confirm the screen does not dim under the default AC-power configuration. Validate battery behavior: disconnect power and confirm the screen dims. Validate power attach behavior: reconnect power and confirm the screen brightens. Record pass/fail results for each check in the test log.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria: Pass: The Surface Brightness Control application installs successfully. The service is running. The registry configuration shows the service enabled and default settings applied. The screen does not dim on AC power under default settings. The screen dims on battery power. The screen brightens when AC power is attached. Fail: The Surface Brightness Control service is not installed or not running. Registry values are not set as expected. The screen does not dim when expected on battery power. The screen does not brighten when AC power is attached. The default brightness behavior does not match the expected configuration.

Set $Answer = $true if the service object exists, otherwise keep $Answer = $false.
Set $TestCaseName = "Confirm the Brightness service is not running."
If the service is not found (!($Answer)), write the test result as Pass.
If the service is found, write the test result as Fail.

Set $Answer = $true if the service exists; otherwise keep $Answer = $false.
Set $TestCaseName = "Confirm the Brightness service running."
If the service exists, write the test result as Pass; otherwise write Fail, log failure, print an error message, and exit.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: TypeCoverDisable

testScenarios.objective: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: TypeCoverDisable
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At each boot after test stage 0, EndOfTestCleanup calls NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState.
NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState reads the initial bad-driver list from the user environment variable DriversNotOK.
It queries current non-OK devices via Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0}.
It filters out devices already bad before the test, leaving only additional bad devices.
If any additional bad devices remain, the helper returns false and the objective is logged as Fail.
If no additional bad devices are found, the objective is logged as Pass.

testCases.testName: No new drivers not OK at start of: TypeCoverDisable

testScenarios.objective: No new drivers not OK at start of: TypeCoverDisable
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Read the baseline bad-driver list from the user environment variable DriversNotOK.
Query current device driver state with:
Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }
Build the list of current drivers with status not OK.
Filter out any drivers whose names were already present in the baseline DriversNotOK list.
If additional new drivers remain, log the names and record a failure result for No new drivers not OK at start of: TypeCoverDisable.
If no new drivers remain, record a pass result.

testCases.testName: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: TypeCoverDisable

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: TypeCoverDisable
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
After the TypeCoverDisable test stage boots, shared cleanup logic calls NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState from TestFunctionality.psm1.
NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState reads the baseline bad-driver list from the DriversNotOK environment variable.
It queries current non-OK devices with Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }.
It filters out drivers already present in the baseline list.
If any new bad drivers remain, it flags a failure; otherwise it records success.
TestResult.psm1 prepends SCPC:  to the objective name when SCPC.dat indicates Secure Core enabled.

testScenarios.detailedSteps:

Call IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest to determine whether the Type Cover keyboard is currently connected.

testCases.testName: SCPC: Verify the Type cover is present

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: Verify the Type cover is present
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Enter Stage 1 and detect whether AutoKVM automation is active using Start-AutoKvmUefiCaptureTask.
If automated, clear AutoKVM status and write an AutoKVM marker log entry.
Call IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest to check whether the Type Cover keyboard is currently connected.
If the Type Cover is found:
Send the SEMM package with -SettingState $false to disable Type Cover.
Log that Type Cover is going to be disabled.
Write the test result Verify the Type cover is present as Pass.
Advance the stage tracker to Stage 2.
If the Type Cover is not found:
Send the SEMM package with -SettingState $true to keep the setting enabled.
Write the test result Verify the Type cover is present as Fail.
Log that no keyboards were found and that Type Cover may already be disabled.
Advance to cleanup stage.

testCases.testName: The TypeCoverDisable test

testScenarios.objective: The TypeCoverDisable test
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Stage 0: ensure the Type Cover is currently enabled; if it is already disabled, enable it and reboot to start from a known default state.
Stage 1: verify the Type Cover is present with IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest; if present, disable it by sending the SEMM package with -SettingState $false; record Verify the Type cover is present Pass.
Stage 2: after reboot with Type Cover disabled, verify it is not present; record Type cover is not present Pass if IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest returns false.
Stage 3: re-enable Type Cover with Send-SemmPackage -SettingState $true, reboot, then verify Type cover is present Pass if IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest returns true.
Stage 4: perform cleanup with EndOfTestCleanup.

Re-enable Type Cover via Send-SemmPackage -SettingState $true -IdNumber $testDataObject.SemmID -ResourcePath $testDataObject.ResourcePath.
Call IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest to detect whether the Type Cover is currently connected.
If no Type Cover is found, write Type cover is not present with status Pass.

If automated, call Get-AutoKVMPassFail -TestName "Type Cover" -TestResultsFileName $testDataObject.TestResultsLogName -DesiredOutput "True".
Call IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest to detect the Type Cover keyboard.
If IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest returns true, write Type cover is present as Pass.
If it returns false, write Type cover is present as Fail.

testCases.testName: Verify the Type cover is present

testScenarios.objective: Verify the Type cover is present
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Enter Stage 1 and start AutoKVM capture with Start-AutoKvmUefiCaptureTask.
If AutoKVM is active, clear AutoKVM status and append a marker to $testDataObject.AutoKVMLog.
Call IsTypeCoverConnected -duringTest to detect the Type Cover.
If the Type Cover is found:
Send Send-SemmPackage -SettingState $false to disable Type Cover.
Log that the Type Cover is being disabled.
Write the result Verify the Type cover is present as Pass.
Advance the stage tracker to Stage 2.
If the Type Cover is not found:
Send Send-SemmPackage -SettingState $true to leave the setting enabled.
Write the result Verify the Type cover is present as Fail.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPages

testScenarios.objective: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPages
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The UEFI Pages test is defined in TestingScript.xml as UEFI Pages with UEFIPages.ps1 in UEFIPages.
After the test stage completes, shared cleanup logic calls NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState.
That helper reads baseline bad drivers from the DriversNotOK user environment variable.
It queries current non-OK devices with:
Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }
It filters out any drivers that were already not OK before the test started.
If any new bad drivers remain, it records a fail result; if none remain, it records a pass.

testCases.testName: No new drivers not OK at start of: UEFIPages

testScenarios.objective: No new drivers not OK at start of: UEFIPages
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Call Set_DriversNotOK_EnvironmentVariable -TestName UEFIPages -ResultsLogForTest <log> from the test startup or shared workflow.
Read the baseline bad-driver names from the DriversNotOK user environment variable.
Query current devices with:
Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }
Build the list of current bad drivers and filter out any whose names are already in the baseline.
If any new bad drivers remain, log them and mark the objective as Fail.
If no new bad drivers remain, mark the objective as Pass.

testCases.testName: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPages

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPages
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
After the test stage boots and the test is supported, shared cleanup logic calls NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState in TestFunctionality.psm1.
NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState reads the baseline bad-device list from the DriversNotOK user environment variable.
It queries current non-OK devices with:
Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }
It filters those current bad devices to remove any whose names were already in the baseline list.
If any new bad drivers remain, the helper returns failure and the result is written as No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPages.
If no new bad drivers remain, the result is written as Pass.
When SCPC mode is enabled, TestResult.psm1 prepends SCPC:  to the result name, producing SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPages.

testCases.testName: SCPC: No new drivers not OK at start of: UEFIPages

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: No new drivers not OK at start of: UEFIPages
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Set_DriversNotOK_EnvironmentVariable is called with $TestName = "UEFIPages" and the current test results log.
Determine the baseline bad-driver names from the DriversNotOK environment variable.
Query current bad drivers with:
Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }
Filter those drivers to exclude any names already present in the baseline.
Save the current bad-driver names back into DriversNotOK.
If any new bad drivers remain and they are not known bugs, write a fail result.
Otherwise, write a pass result.
If SCPC is enabled, TestResult.psm1 prepends SCPC:  to the result name.

testScenarios.objective: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPassword
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At the start of the UEFIPassword run, Get-TestStarted captures baseline bad drivers via Set_DriversNotOK_EnvironmentVariable:
Query Win32_PNPEntity devices where Status -ne "OK" and ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0.
Save the baseline driver names into the DriversNotOK user environment variable.
On subsequent test stages after the initial boot, Get-TestStarted calls NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState.
NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState:
Queries current Win32_PNPEntity drivers with non-OK status and an error code.
Filters out drivers already present in the baseline DriversNotOK list.
Returns any newly bad drivers introduced after test start.
The shared logic then writes the result:
Write-TestResult -Name "No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPassword" -Status ...

testScenarios.objective: No new drivers not OK at start of: UEFIPassword
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
When UEFIPassword begins, Get-TestStarted in TestFunctionality.psm1 runs the initial test setup.
If the test stage tracker file does not exist, the framework calls Set_DriversNotOK_EnvironmentVariable -TestName $testName -ResultsLogForTest $testData.LogName.
That helper:
Reads the prior baseline driver names from the DriversNotOK environment variable.
Queries current devices with Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }.
Filters out any drivers already present in the baseline.
Saves the current non-OK driver names back into DriversNotOK.
Writes the result named No new drivers not OK at start of: UEFIPassword.

testCases.testName: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPassword

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: UEFIPassword

The test proceeds through password enable/disable stages and reboots as defined in UEFIPassword.ps1.
After stage 0, on subsequent boots (TestStage -ne 0), NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState is evaluated.

testCases.testName: The USBCPorts test

testScenarios.objective: The USBCPorts test
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
Import shared test library from $SolutionBasePath\Library\TestLibrary.psm1.
Determine the test name from the script file name: USBCPorts.
Initialize test execution state with Get-TestStarted -testName $testName -finalTestStage $finalTestStage.

Query supported USB-C SEMM IDs with GetSupportedSemmIDs -semmIdList $testDataObject.SemmID.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: USBPorts

testScenarios.objective: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: USBPorts
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At test runtime, after the initial stage, the helper reads the start-of-test bad-driver baseline from the DriversNotOK environment variable.
It queries current device driver status with Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 }.
It filters out drivers that were already not OK at test start.
It uses the remaining list to determine whether any additional devices are now in a bad state.
It then writes the result for No additional devices ended up in bad state in: USBPorts.

testCases.testName: No new drivers not OK at start of: USBPorts

testScenarios.objective: No new drivers not OK at start of: USBPorts
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At test startup the framework stores any drivers already not OK into the DriversNotOK environment variable (Set_DriversNotOK_EnvironmentVariable).
When the check runs, call Get-CimInstance Win32_PNPEntity | Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "OK" } | Where-Object { $_.ConfigManagerErrorCode -gt 0 } to list current non-OK drivers.
Filter out drivers present in the start-of-test baseline (DriversNotOK).
Return the remaining list from NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState and use it to determine the objective result.

testCases.testName: Number of USB devices matches start of test

The script then records the result as either pass or fail based on whether the counts match.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: the current number of USB devices equals the count recorded at the start of the test.
Fail: the current number of USB devices does not match the starting count. In the script, if the count is lower, it also notes that the expected USB 3.0 device may be missing.

testCases.testName: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: USBPorts

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: USBPorts
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
At the beginning of the test, the framework captures any drivers that are already in a non-OK state and stores that information for comparison.
After the test has progressed beyond the initial stage, the check evaluates whether any additional devices entered a bad state.
It uses the helper logic for “NoAdditionalDevicesInBadState” and reviews the returned device list.
If the resulting device issue is not one of the known, intentionally ignored driver bugs, the framework logs a failure; otherwise it records a pass.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: no additional devices are found in a bad state after the test, or any such devices are part of the known ignored-bug list.
Fail: one or more additional devices are found in a bad state after the test, and the issue is not in the known ignore list.

testCases.testName: SCPC: No new drivers not OK at start of: USBPorts

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: No new drivers not OK at start of: USBPorts
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The framework captures the initial baseline of drivers that are already in a non-OK state and have a non-zero ConfigManagerErrorCode.
It then compares the current driver list against that baseline during the USBPorts test flow.
If any new drivers are found in a bad state, the check reviews them against the known-driver-bug ignore list.
The result is then written as either a pass or fail entry for the test log.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: no new drivers appear in a non-OK state beyond the baseline from the start of the test, or any such findings are recognized as known/ignored device-driver bugs.
Fail: one or more new drivers enter a non-OK state during the test, and the issue is not covered by the known-bug ignore list.

testCases.testName: SCPC: Number of USB devices matches start of test

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: Number of USB devices matches start of test

It compares the current count to the previously recorded starting count.
The result is then written to the test results log as Pass or Fail.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: the current USB device count is equal to the count recorded at the start of the test.
Fail: the current USB device count does not match the starting count. The script also logs an additional note if the count is lower, indicating that the expected USB device may be missing.

testCases.testName: SCPC: The USBPorts test

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: The USBPorts test
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The script verifies that the relevant SEMM IDs for USB-A or USB-C are supported and enabled.
It prompts the user to remove existing USB devices, then connects USB devices and verifies that they appear on the enabled port.
It disables the ports through SEMM, reboots, and verifies that the connected devices are no longer present or no longer enumerate as expected.
It re-enables the ports, reboots again, and checks that the USB device count returns to the same count observed at the start of the test.
It also checks for any new device-driver issues that appear during the SCPC test run.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: the USB ports can be toggled between enabled and disabled states correctly, USB devices enumerate as expected, the final USB device count matches the starting count, and no new device or driver issues appear beyond the known ignored cases.
Fail: the ports do not behave correctly when toggled, USB devices do not appear or disappear as expected, the final device count differs from the start-of-test count, or new devices/drivers enter a bad state during the test.

testCases.testName: SCPC: Verify USB is not present when disabled

testScenarios.objective: SCPC: Verify USB is not present when disabled
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The script records the USB device count that was present before the ports were disabled.
After the ports are disabled and the system reboots, it collects the current USB device count again.
It compares the new count with the previously recorded count.
If the count is lower, the script treats that as the expected result for a disabled port.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: the current USB device count is lower than the count recorded before the ports were disabled, showing that the USB device is no longer present when the port is disabled.
Fail: the current USB device count is unchanged or still at the same level as before, indicating that the device remained present despite the disabled state.

testCases.testName: The USBPorts test

testScenarios.objective: The USBPorts test
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The test checks whether the relevant USB SEMM IDs are supported on the device.
It prompts the user to remove existing USB devices and then connects a USB device to verify that it appears on the enabled port.
It disables the USB ports through SEMM, reboots, and verifies that the device is no longer present or no longer enumerates while the port is disabled.
It re-enables the ports, reboots again, and verifies that the USB device count returns to the starting count.
It also performs SCPC-related checks to ensure no new device-driver issues are introduced during the test.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: the USB ports can be toggled between enabled and disabled states correctly, devices appear when enabled and disappear when disabled, the final device count matches the start-of-test count, and no new bad driver/device states are introduced.
Fail: any of the expected USB behavior fails, such as the device not appearing when the port is enabled, remaining present when the port is disabled, or the final device count not matching the starting count, or if new device/driver problems appear during the test.

testCases.testName: Verify USB is not present when disabled

testScenarios.objective: Verify USB is not present when disabled
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The script records the USB device count before the port is disabled.
It sends the SEMM package to disable the relevant USB port(s) and reboots the device.
After reboot, it measures the current USB device count again.
It compares the new count to the count recorded before the disable action.
If the count decreases, that indicates the device is no longer present when the port is disabled.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: the device count after disabling is lower than the pre-disable count, showing the USB device is no longer present when the port is disabled.
Fail: the device count remains the same or does not decrease, meaning the device is still present despite the port being disabled.

Stage 0 sets up the test and may disable a previously enabled setting before rebooting.

Stage 4 runs cleanup and completes the test.

Fail: the SEMM setting is not in the expected state at any of those checks.

testCases.testName: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: WifiBt

testScenarios.objective: No additional devices ended up in bad state in: WifiBt
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The framework records the baseline of devices/drivers that were already in a non-OK state before the WifiBt test started.
It runs the WifiBt test flow, which changes the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth state and verifies the expected enable/disable transitions.
After the test completes, it compares the post-test device status to the pre-test baseline.
It also checks for known device-driver bug exceptions before deciding whether to fail the objective.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: if no additional devices/drivers enter a bad state beyond the baseline, or if the only issues are known exempted device-driver bugs, the objective is recorded as Pass for “No additional devices ended up in bad state in: WifiBt”.
Fail: if one or more new devices/drivers appear in a bad state and they are not covered by the known-bug exception logic, the objective is recorded as Fail.

testCases.testName: No new drivers not OK at start of: WifiBt

testScenarios.objective: No new drivers not OK at start of: WifiBt
testScenarios.detailedSteps:
The framework collects the current set of PnP devices/drivers whose status is not “OK” and whose configuration manager error code is greater than zero.
It compares that list to the baseline of drivers already known to be non-OK from the start of the test, stored in the DriversNotOK environment variable.
It identifies any new non-OK drivers that were not part of the original baseline.
It then writes the result to the WifiBt test log as either Pass or Fail, while ignoring known device-driver bug exceptions when applicable.
testScenarios.passFailCriteria:
Pass: if no new drivers beyond the initial baseline are found in a non-OK state, or if only known exempted device-driver bugs are present, the result is recorded as Pass for “No new drivers not OK at start of: WifiBt”.
Fail: if one or more new drivers appear in a non-OK state and they are not covered by the known-bug exception logic, the result is recorded as Fail for that objective.
